stem: In a certain code language, CAT is written as DBU. Using the same rule, how is DOG written in that code?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Shifting only the first and second letters by +1 but leaving G unchanged gives EPG, misapplying the rule to only two of the three letters.
The rule is: each letter is shifted forward by 1 position in the alphabet. D+1=E, O+1=P, G+1=H. So DOG becomes EPH.
Shifting D by +2 instead of +1 gives F for the first letter, resulting in FPH instead of EPH.
Shifting D+1=E correctly but O+2=Q (adding 2 instead of 1 to O) and G+1=H gives EQH, misapplying the shift inconsistently.

explanation: Checking the given code: C(3)+1=D(4), A(1)+1=B(2), T(20)+1=U(21). So CAT becomes DBU by adding 1 to each letter's position. Applying the same rule to DOG: D+1=E, O+1=P, G+1=H. The code for DOG is EPH.

explanation_sections.punchline: The single consistent rule is +1 shift to every letter, verified across all three letters of the example before applying it.
explanation_sections.approach: Apply clues most-certain-first: decode each letter of the example (C->D, A->B, T->U) to confirm the rule; shift = +1 for all letters. Apply to DOG: D->E, O->P, G->H. Answer: EPH.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always verify the coding rule on all letters of the given example before applying it; a rule that works for only one letter may be a coincidence.
explanation_sections.timing: 20 seconds. Verify rule on example (3 checks), apply to target (3 shifts). Trap: inconsistent shifting (applying +2 to some letters) or leaving one letter unchanged.
